en: Preface to the Catalogue of the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuming Huixing of the Great Song,
composed by Yan Yiqi (Ruxun).
The Record of the Sayings of Zifú Chán Monastery in Qízhōu;
the Record of the Sayings of Zhìdù Chán Monastery on North Mountain in Qízhōu;
and the Record of the Sayings of Néngrén Chán Monastery on Mount Lúshān in Nánkāng Commandery.
Record of the Sayings at Kāśyapa Flower-Treasury Chan Monastery, Kaixian, Mount Lu, Nankang Prefecture;
Record of the Sayings at Baojue Chan Monastery, Qixian, Mount Lu, Nankang Prefecture;
Record of the Sayings at Zunxiang Chan Monastery, Yangshan, Pingjiang Prefecture.
Record of Sayings, Verses on Ancient Cases, Dharma Words, True Portraits, Testaments, and Epitaph for the Chan Master of Shouning Wansui Temple at the Twin Pagodas in Pingjiang Prefecture.
Composed by the Layman Yan Yiqi (Ruxun).

Postscript to the Recorded Sayings of Zen Master Wuzhun of Jingshan Postscript by Zen Master Beijian of Jingci Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Venerable Xing of Wuming The single lineage of Dongshan has incurred the greatest resentment from others.
Those who rely on the literal text mostly interpret it as ordinary or as something extraordinary.
"This is a phrase of life; that is a phrase of death. Such mutual distinctions between the skillful and the clumsy all fall into conceptual traps.
Even if one manages to leap out, one still falls into the deep pit of liberation. This does not merely mean missing the mark regarding this old master;
it means missing the mark regarding all the old monks of the world. It only serves to add more volumes and increase the poison. Because I have commented on Wuming’s words, I... [text ends]
I am aware that you are talkative and fear there may be those who are soft-headed or stubborn; even for the sake of a single vegetarian feast and repentance, they do not perceive it.
On the Shangji day of the Gui-mao year of Chunyou (1243), Yan Ruxun respectfully wrote this at a vegetarian feast in Changzhou.
This is the record of the sermons from Zifu Chan Temple in Qi Prefecture.
Compiled by Attendant Miaoyan.
Upon entering the monastery, he points to the mountain gate and says: "Ten thousand layers of peaks and ridges are exquisite, amidst the pure, empty, and distant mists.
That single phrase for crossing the gate—should one hesitate, they are separated by a heavy barrier."
Incense is offered in the Buddha Hall; pointing to heaven, pointing to earth—what point is there in this? Looking around in all four directions, one does not realize the loss has been incurred.
This brings trouble upon descendants for generations to come, as they thus pass on a state of mutual dullness and neglect.
Seated within the square fathom, like lightning flashing and thunder rolling, he uses poison to counter poison, scatters earth and flings sand, and forces the straight into a curve.
Here, one must turn the body around to draw the horned bow; who can reach back behind the head to pull out the golden arrowhead?
The Dharma-seat clouds: one knows not by how much its standing place is high. Turning the head and looking around, white clouds hang low.
In an ordinary step, one ascends to the crown of Vairocana; pulling back the Southern Dipper, one establishes it in the west.

Holding up his robe, he said: "If you wish to join the herd of oxen, you must still don the hide of a water-buffalo. Moving entirely within the ranks of other species, you pull the plow and guide the team.
He ascended the seat. Having finished offering incense to pray for the Emperor, he next held up the incense and said: "This single portion of incense was formerly offered by me to Foguo Fozhao."
From Chan Master [Xuedou] he obtained the essence; from Master Songyuan he obtained the function.
Although he was thus complete in both essence and function, he drifted through the lakes and seas without a single person offering a fair price for him.

Now, as "one guest need not trouble two hosts," he burns this incense in the furnace to honor his late teacher, the former Abbot of Lingyin in Lin’an Prefecture, thereby repaying the milk of the Dharma.
He then adjusted his robes and took his seat. A monk asked, "The dragons and elephants have gathered from the four quarters and you have ascended the precious throne;
as a student, I come before you and request that you offer prayers for the Emperor. The Master replied, "The One Breath speaks not, yet it contains all forms;

where could the myriad spirits go to express their gratitude for this impartiality? The monk pressed further, "What is the phrase that secures the essential ford? The Master said, "To deliberate is already an error—white clouds."
Wanli asked, “What is the phrase that cuts off heaven and earth? The Master said, “The heavens are high and the myriad phenomena are correct;
the seas are vast and the hundred rivers flow toward them. He asked, “What is the phrase that cuts off the heads of the Reward and Transformation Buddhas?

The Master said, “When the Great Function manifests, no fixed rules remain. He asked, “How is it when one proceeds in this very way? The Master said, “Go and investigate further for three [more days].”
[The Master] had been practicing for thirty years. A monk prostrated, and the Master said: "Having traveled the long and winding road to its end, there is no mountain that is not home.
That single phrase for crossing the gate—should you hesitate, it lies across the heavens. The four mountains are vast and open; a single path is secluded and deep.

The pavilions and towers rise majestically, and the peaks and ridges are layered with emerald green. All of this is one's own original ground, revealing the ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas. It cannot be avoided.
Hanging the alms-bag high, breaking off the staff, settling one’s home and finding joy in one’s work, drumming the belly and singing songs—this is the livelihood that requires no further seeking.

As for the gathering of mountain birds, the wagging of a cow’s tail, the tiger’s roar and the dragon’s chant, the clarity of the wind and the whiteness of the dew, the streams, mountains, clouds, and moon—everywhere the same breeze;
the waterfowl and the forest trees—each and every thing reveals the truth. Now tell me: what is this?
"How can one speak upon the single phrase 'Shared Joy in Peace'? He turned the Shaolin "Pierced-less Flute" upside down, blowing it against the wind and then with the wind.
Again, he cited the case where Baoshou opened the hall; Sansheng pushed forward a monk, and Baoshou struck him immediately. The Master said, "I thought..."
Hou Bai. There is also Hou Hei. Sansheng said, "To act as a teacher in such a manner not only blinds this monk’s eyes, but will blind the eyes of everyone in the city of Zhenzhou.
The Master said, "The thief must be caught by the thief. Baoshou then returned to his quarters.
The Master said, "The tiger's head and the tiger's tail are both captured at once. If you all wish to recognize where these two great elders fell [into error]..."
"Where? He struck his staff once and said, "When the wind ceases, the flowers still fall; when the birds cry, the mountains grow more secluded.
He ascended the hall and said, "Within words there are no words; thus, for nine years, Bodhidharma sat in vain facing the wall. Within no-words there are words."
"Empty space gives birth to flowers by the crags, strewn in profusion. When both existence and non-existence have vanished, how can one proceed?

"The Southern Dipper has eight; the Northern Dipper has seven. Entering the hall, he said: "My mouth is silenced and my tongue is made bald; even an enlightened monk finds it difficult to discern. Thereupon, he cast down [the whisk].
Holding up his staff, he said: "Today, I scatter it before everyone; Mount Sumeru and King Lamp-Wielder cannot stop laughing.
He then ascended the hall and said: "Citing Yunmen’s instruction to the assembly: 'The weather is cold and the days are short; two people share one bowl. The Master said:"
The Yunmen tradition is too frugal. Zifu, however, is not so. "The sky is cold and the days are short; three parts full, two parts full.
A tiger bites a tiger; a rooster lays an egg. Tell me, what matter does this clarify? Investigate!

The Head Administrative Officer (Zhishi) Xie ascended the hall and said: "Amidst the roar of a sudden thunderclap, within the flash of a lightning bolt, the staff and the shout fly back and forth, and host and guest manifest one another.
At this very moment, tell me: whose wind and moon is this? Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he said:
"A few fragments of white clouds arise in the universe; throughout the heavens, there is nowhere they do not cast their shade."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When words are uttered, they are not sounds; the tongue has no bone. Before forms appear, there is no object; the foxes still cling to their den.
Ultimately, what is the phrase that does not fall into sound or form? Where the partridge cries, the flowers of a hundred kinds are fragrant."
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhidu of Beishan Zhisu Temple in Qizhou, Compiled by Attendant Yuan Cheng.
Ascending the Hall, he said: "Fresh plum blossoms break forth faintly amidst the snow; The loving sun gradually lengthens before the window. Leaking forth the East..."
"Good news for you! It is clearly manifest throughout the entire realm and cannot be hidden. But tell me, what is it that cannot be hidden?
He struck the ground with his staff and said: "Once you have reached the stable ground of your own home, there is no more Buddha-dharma to deliberate upon."
Ascending the hall, he said: "At the absolute summit of Niujia, we enter the retreat for the summer rains. Encompassing all that exists, it swallows the ten directions.
Now tell me, where is the True Person of No Rank? After a long silence, he said: "Be careful not to seek it from others; to do so would distance you from me."
Upon returning from the city, he ascended the hall and said: "Coming and going are without interval; movement and stillness share a single source. In a flash one departs, and in a flash one returns.
In the Great Dharma there is neither interior nor exterior—what need is there to distinguish between the new year and the old?
Having returned, I lie prostrate beneath the green pines; this very thing is subtle and cannot be transmitted."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Just as we are drawing in the fresh spring, we again welcome the vermilion summer. The mountain is not made high by it, nor the water made low.
The plum rains stretch on and on, pasting a hexagram across the void. The stone tortoise is soaked and rotten; the yellow plum season adds further talk.
At the summit of Mount Wuya, waves surge to the heavens; the Rhinoceros Fan increases its value."
Ascending the hall, the Master cited a poem by Hanshan: "My mind is like the autumn moon, / A clear and bright pool in the azure depths.
/ Nothing can be compared to it; / How am I to describe it? The Master said, "Hanshan sits trapped in a deep pit of liberation.
If he were under the gate of Beishan, we would strike his head until it is shattered and his forehead split open."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The autumn wind is clear; the autumn moon is white. Geese pass through the vast sky; cicadas chirp among the courtyard cypresses.

Kicking out the Iron Kunlun, the great pivot of function is suddenly unleashed. To scar good flesh is to dig a wound; to look upon it is to go blind. A man beyond the mountains sings a song of Great Peace;
it is originally nothing but the eighteen variations of the Hu flute."

Ascending the hall, he said: "A refreshing air arises in the sleeves; a clear breeze sweeps through the four quarters. White clouds embrace the secluded rocks; how cold and yet how pure and extraordinary!
Eight facets of crystalline clarity naturally encircle one another; who would dare to peer into this steep and lofty singular peak?"
Ascending the hall on account of a matter: "A venomous snake can scratch its own head; this is precisely our family’s kitchen-leaper. He has stolen these meager skills;
with a hand that plunders by daylight, he seeks advantage. [口@力]. Standing alone on one foot atop a ten-thousand-fathom cliff.
"A head three feet long—know who this is?
He ascended the hall and said: "Before the fifteenth day, 'one winter, two winters,' with hands folded across the chest. After the fifteenth day..."
With his back turned, he draws the golden-tipped arrow; with a somersault, he grips the horned bow. At this very moment of the fifteenth day, what is it like?
"The wind follows the tiger, and the clouds follow the dragon. Raising his eyes, a hawk flies past Liaodong.
Record of the Sayings of Chan Master Nengren of Guizong Monastery on Mount Lu, Nanjiang Prefecture.
Compiled by Attendant Miaochuan.

Ascending the Dharma Hall, he said: "Spring travels through the myriad lands, yet spring leaves no trace; only when the winter snows have melted does its efficacy become manifest. It responds in every single thing."
It is currently circulating everywhere: the wooden horse and the clay ox bellow; the flowers and willows shake in the spring breeze.
He ascended the hall and said: "The spring mountains are green; the spring waters are lush. The grass is thick and the flowers cluster.
If you can utterly exhaust the functioning of the senses before you, you will see the true face of Mount Lu."

Ascending the hall, he said: "On the fifteenth day of the first month, the Lantern Festival, golden lotuses appear everywhere. Yet, in greedily gazing at the Buddha of Lamp-Light, one misses the arrow from Silla.
Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he said: "Within a flash of lightning, a single thread is briefly made to pass through."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The willow color holds mist; a thousand blossoms vie for beauty. The myriad phenomena of the forest and the heavens mutually manifest the family style.
The True Person of No Rank lies across the entire realm. At this very moment, what is it like? He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and said:
The whale swallows the seawater until it is exhausted, revealing the coral branches.

Speaking from the high seat as the Head Seat (Shouzuo) and Director of the Seat (Dianshuo), he said: "The pillars of the Dharma community and the discipline of the monastic groves consist entirely of killing and entirely of bringing life."

Establishing the fundamental principle: releasing both and gathering both simultaneously—altogether it is right here. When the tiger roars, the wind arises; when the dragon cries, the mist rises. Striking the whisk, he says:
"Everyone, help lift up this broken sand pot! Boundless refreshing breezes continue to arrive without end."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The phrase within the phrase cuts off all proclamations; amidst a flash of lightning, one distinguishes the black from the white. But tell me:
when the Purple Cloud Peak is high and the Luan River water is swift, how does one distinguish black from white? Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he said:
"Dai Song’s ox lies in the shade of the green willows; Han Gan’s horse neighs at the ford of fragrant grass."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The path leading upward is slippery; it stands ten thousand fathoms high, sheer and precipitous. The flash of a spark or a streak of lightning is dull.
The phrase that settles heaven and earth is mistaken. After a long silence, he said: "The water buffalo always delights in water and grass; the qilin has but a single horn."
"The thousand hands of Great Compassion are difficult to grasp.
The Abbot, thanking the administrative officials, ascended the hall and said: "The host within the guest; the guest within the host. The great tiger of the Southern Mountain is originally a panther.
Raising the eyebrows, look with your own eyes. Seize the opportunity quickly amidst a flash of lightning! He struck the whisk and said: "To trigger the mechanism, one must..."
"This is a crossbow capable of piercing a thousand *jin*.
Entering the hall, he said: "One who knows this has a speck of dust in their eye; even if they overturn everything to the bottom, they will only obtain a single fragment.
It is truly laughable that the old, ancient fellow of Ba Ling could say, 'Silver bowls filled with snow.'"
Ascending the hall, he said: "That which cannot be spoken from a full mouth leaves the patriarchs of the world with nothing but tongues tied.
That which cannot be seen with full eyes, one encounters in every lantern and pillar. That which cannot be heard with full ears—when the bell tolls and the drum resounds, avoid picking at it!
Do not pick at it! Otherwise, you will extinguish the True Dharma Eye of Linji. Where would you put that broken sand pot?"

Ascending the hall, he said: "Guizong saw that the merchandise was already complete; there was no separate 'mind-essence' to be transmitted. At the two meal times, they unfold their bowls and open their mats;
day after day, they relieve themselves of excrement and urine. Eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty—everything is the same.
The pillar and the lantern laugh aloud! But tell me, what are they laughing at? Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon it long ago, yet until this very day, he has not attained the wondrous."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The wind whistles and the leaves fall from the sparse forest; the moon is bright and clear as tigers roar and monkeys cry.
Whether heard or seen, whether awakened or deluded—whether one understands or not—it is the total, complete presentation of the whole body. The nostrils have always been hanging downward."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to all under heaven; when a single speck of dust rises, the great earth is gathered up.

Clear and manifest is the intent of the Patriarchs; clear and manifest is the tip of every blade of grass. Buying a hat to fit a head; looking at the tower and striking the tower. He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and said:
"What more could one wish for that is not elegant?"

Ascending the hall, he said: "Autumn colors join the heavens in purity; autumn flowers fill the earth with fragrance. The Gate of Perfect Penetration stands wide open—take care not to deliberate wrongly.
Ascending the hall for the opening of the furnace, he said: "Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, and the temple master’s eyebrows and beard fell out. Both are iron nails without holes."
Hammer! When both sides err, they follow along with the error. A scorched brick strikes the frozen ground to its very bottom. One laughs at Puhua shaking his bell. Entering the hall, he said:
"Snow covers the thousand mountains, yet the solitary peak is not white. It stands out, yet is difficult to discern; look at it and you are blind. Iron.
The tree flowers bloom; the ice river erupts in flame. Upon the ungerminating branch, the moon is at its third watch. One must by all means avoid having one's scales marked at the Dragon Gate.
Entering the hall, he said: "Flapping lips and wagging tongues, unfolding matters to meet the occasion—even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, there would be no way to repent. Return.
The school [of Zen] knows this yet deliberately violates it. You people, where do you fix your eyes? Striking with the whisk in a gesture of meditation, he said:
"Burnt! Burnt! Leaves but no branches. The long sky and autumn waters; solitary wild geese and setting clouds."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Guizong has no dharma to deliberate upon; he simply holds up the single point without concealment.
If you ask about the essential meaning of the Western Come, the sky is cold, the days are short, and the nights are especially long."
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-Bathing ceremony, he said: Pointing to heaven, pointing to earth, he alone claims supremacy; He stirs up heaven and earth, and the seas and mountains grow dark.
Since then, he has deceived countless people, Until this very day, no one has a "brain-door."
Ascending the hall, he said: "After the rain has passed through the vast sky, drops drip from the eaves. This is presented face-to-face, yet people cannot believe it.
If they can believe it, the eternal sky has never been wet."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The one is all; all is the one. To take up Qingyufxia and place it within the eye of a tiny gnat, or to grasp the great earth and bring it here like a grain of millet—if you understand this, then all things are of one family; if you do not understand, then know that I am being wronged."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Standing alone, it marks out the myriad phenomena; beyond all things, it proclaims the truth. Holding up his staff, he said: "Heaven is long-lasting, earth is long-lasting; earth is long-lasting, heaven is long-lasting. Ascending the hall again, he said:
"Without action and without effort, without speech and without demonstration, one can thereby save the multitudes and unify the ten thousand states. Together...
The six realms of emptiness merge with the three periods of time. (He plants his staff upright and says: "This is the primary principle of our house.
Compiled by Attendant Daolong from the *Recorded Sayings* of Kai-xian Hua-zang Chan Monastery on Mount Lu, Nan-kang Commandery.
Entering the monastery, he points to the mountain gate and says: "A waterfall hangs from a precipice, falling into the midst of space; At ease, one strides across the Guanghan Palace.
Seizing the moment, one sits and cuts off all at the peak of the solitary crag; Let the thousand sages be made to stand in the lee of the wind."
The Buddha Hall Inscription states: "When the ancestors do not resolve [the matter], their descendants suffer the consequences. Wherever one prays or strikes, there is nowhere to evade it.
Though they do not decline to prostrate and burn incense, they also seek to mutually obstruct one another."
The Abbot said: "This is the furnace and forge of a master; it is the essential hammer and tongs. There is no need to set ambushes or lay traps;
one seeks advantage within the hands of a master thief."
The Dharma Seat Master said: "A shout scatters the white clouds; it pierces through the azure void. With every step, one advances further; with every move, one rises higher.
Having ascended the seat and finished the prayer for the Emperor, he sat down and said: "Before a word is raised, who can discuss what is already known? It overturns the seas and mountains."
Moving heaven and earth. Turning one’s body within the words of the precipitous cliff. The disk rolls the pearl, and the pearl rolls the disk. A monk asked, "What is the Linji school?
The Master said, "A thunderclap too swift to cover the ears. The monk pressed further, "What is the Guiyang school?
The Master said, "Father and son do not transmit it to one another. The monk pressed further, "What is the Yunmen school? The Master said, "The sword."

"It has been long since he departed; you are merely laboring in vain by marking the boat. The student asked, "What is the Cao-Dong school? The Master said, "Within the shadows of white clouds, strange rocks are revealed;
amidst the radiance of flowing water, ancient trees remain green. The student asked, "What is the Fa-Yan school?

The Master said, "Outside the mind there is no dharma; before one's eyes are the green mountains. The student said, "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the various schools. As for that which transcends them—"
"What is the matter with the vehicle of our school? The Master said, "The flowers must bloom throughout the night; do not wait for the morning breeze to blow.

The monk further asked, "Tell me, yesterday there was the Elder of Guizong; today there is the Master of Kaixian. What is the ultimate reality here? The Master said, "Both ends are completely severed;
a single sword leans against the cold heavens. The monk bowed. The Master spoke again: "The harmonious atmosphere fills the heavens."
The springtime radiance of the earth overflows the eyes; bright brilliance shines upon all things. Mountain flowers are like brocade; stream waters are like indigo.
Butterflies cling to fragrant clusters, manifesting the uncarved heart-seal; orioles sing at the valley mouth, expounding the wondrous gate of non-speaking.
Fully upholding the "Flower-holding" of Vulture Peak, he reveals the secret intent of the Westward Coming. If one proceeds in this very manner, every place is Maitreya.
No gate, no Sudhana. This very place is the field of great peace and bliss; this very place is the arena of great liberation.
Although it is so, how can one finally express the phrase "Together rejoicing in the unconditioned"?
[With the whisk, he strikes the meditation seat. "The accumulation of merit adorned by pure wisdom; the ten-thousand-year-old pine atop Mount Zhurong."
Again, Yushan addressed the assembly, saying, "Call the śrāmaṇera here for me. An attendant monk asked, "Why call the śrāmaṇera?
Yushan said, "I have a broken-legged cauldron; I want him to carry it up and down. The Master [Xuedou] comments: "Frugality breeds unfiliality; righteousness emerges from years of plenty.
To hold it forth face-to-face, there is a standard in the presence of all. Why? Because the whale swallows the sea.
The water has run dry, revealing the coral branches.

On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, he ascended the hall and said: "One Reality contains the Dharma-realm; its great function is equal to empty space. A thousand auspicious signs gather like mist."
Myriad virtues arrive like gathering clouds. (He plants his staff upright and says: "To pray for the immeasurable longevity of our Emperor:
Heaven is high and boundless, Earth is infinite. He ascends the hall and says:
"After the rain falls over the fields and plains, the spring day is bright and serene. The peach is red and the plum is white; they manifest the supreme faculty. *A*! (He remains silent.)
His mouth was closed and his eyebrows were cast down. Among them all, one melody is the excellence of Jiangnan: the reed flute plays in wild, chaotic harmony with the wind.
He ascended the hall and said, "The single phrase prior to sound is manifest throughout the ten directions; Buddhas and Patriarchs do not know it, and monks have no recourse for it.
He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Ten thousand valleys and a thousand crags, where clouds and mists lock together; yet all is transparently clear. It is handed over face-to-face.

Is there anyone here who knows the timing and discerns what is appropriate? After a long silence, he said: "The shadow of the wild geese falls into the cold pool; a solitary boat rests across the wilderness crossing."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Teacher of Vairocana, the Lord of the Dharmakāya—though he may grant or withhold according to the occasion, to whom among those present could even a fraction of this be entrusted?
Kick up your eyebrows and quickly take it up!"

Ascending the hall, he said: "The time since the Sage departed is remote; people are mostly indolent. When met with adversity, they give rise to anger; when met with favor, they give rise to attachment.
Neither angry nor attached—this is the scissors of the Eastern Sea and the cloth bag of the Western Barbarians. At the gate of liberation, fasten the bolt securely;
do not boast that your shop has no one to buy from you. After a long pause, he said: "Seeing the cheek behind the head, the culprit is caught with the stolen goods."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A fresh autumn rain brings a fresh chill; The roads are dustless, and the wild chrysanthemums are fragrant.
I laugh instead at the former Magistrate Tao, Who frowned and returned home—a miscalculation. Whether it be "thus" or "not thus," A broken mirror does not regain its light.
If you take the plucking of flowers and the subtle smile To be the truth, you must strictly avoid calling a servant "Master."
Ascending the hall, he held his staff crosswise and said, "He plays the stringless lute. Then, making the gesture of blowing a flute, he said, "He blows the holeless flute.
"Together we enjoy the age of Yao and the days of Shun; yet Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years in vain."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "If you lift it up, heaven turns and earth revolves; light shines everywhere.
If you set it down, thoughts cease and conditions are forgotten; both sages and ordinary people are at a loss for what to do. But as for not lifting it up and not setting it down—how is that?
He struck the ground once with the staff and said: "The kingfisher tramples through the rain on lotus leaves; the heron breaks through the mist among the green willows."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Long rains have not cleared; as soon as it clears, it rains again. Yin and yang are in harmonious union, and all things find their proper place.

Clearly manifest at the head of the hundred grasses, you are able to be the sovereign of the myriad phenomena. Striking the seat with his whisk, he said: "Presented face-to-face—take care not to be muddled."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The autumn wind blows steadily; the autumn colors linger. Autumn clouds float serenely; the autumn moon divides its radiance.
This seal of the mind, uncarved like ancient characters, resembles the mechanism of an iron ox. A-he-he! Its power is rare.
Only after repeated searching and grasping will you begin to know."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The moon hangs in the vast sky; dwelling alone upon the solitary peak, the cries of the secluded birds are clear and pure.
Where the white clouds break, they continue on again. Difficult even for the Buddha-eye to perceive, the straight is bent into a curve. When the wild sheep hang their horns, all traces are lost.
Boundless pure breezes arise throughout the eight directions."

On the anniversary of Master Songyuan’s death, he ascended the hall and said: "To eliminate even this phrase, and to eliminate even that which is not a phrase—obscure, muddled, and dull, like a gate-sill of cast iron.
To appear in the world and act for others in such a manner is to blind the true eye of the monks.
If one examines it closely, it is still like Xu Liu carrying a single board."
Record of the Sermons at Qixian Baojue Chan Monastery on Mount Lu, Nanjiang Circuit, compiled by Attendant Yuanzhao. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The nest knows the wind; the burrow knows the rain. This is what worldly people know. But as for the World-Honored One raising [the flower]..."
Flower. Kāśyapa smiled. Tell me, who is it that knows this? He planted his staff and said: "The wooden horse neighs in the forest;
the clay ox bellows at the bottom of the sea."
The Buddha, having attained the Way, ascended the hall and said: "Gautama saw the morning star at midnight; the tip of the pestle pried open the sinew within his eyes.
For forty-nine years he preached fearlessly, yet to this day people mistake the markings on the scale-pan. If one does not lead with a resolute head, they bring ruin upon their entire army.
The waves of Caoxi are just like this: countless ordinary people are submerged and lost."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The grasses grow lush and the smoke drifts vast; the rain is like fat, the clouds like cranes. Having finished speaking—mistake, mistake, mistake!
The Five Elders’ Peak is so high it pierces the bone with cold; the wild monkeys cry out until the mountain moon falls."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Heaven attains the One; Earth attains the One. When the King attains the One, there is no equal to him. If the One has already attained the One, what further need is there?
Amidst the flash of lightning, a thunderclap is added. In the morning, fine rain falls upon the perilous heights; from all eight directions, the pure wind shines upon the red sun."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Great encompasses that which has no exterior; the minute enters that which has no interval. Within and without, all flaws are severed;

from ancient times to the present, there is no front or back. The myriad phenomena of the forested world are hidden within the shadow; the four sages and six classes of beings appear within the light.
Clearly and constantly before you all—do you see it or not? He struck the meditation staff and said: "Through the iron wall and silver mountain, a single thread passes."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Snow buries the pine paths; plum blossoms cling to the cold branches. Bare and naked, bright and unadorned, standing alone with singular distinction.
When Hanshan meets Shide, they clap their hands and laugh heartily."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The first and third days of the month, the ninth of the middle ten days, and the seventh of the final ten days—without further concealment, I bring them forth directly before you.
Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he said: "With a single breath, the great mechanism is turned; in all eight directions, the realm of longevity opens."
On the first day of the first month of the year, he ascended the hall and said: "The moon of mind is solitary and perfect; its pure radiance is bright and clear.

It swallows up the emptiness of the ten directions—like snow placed within a silver bowl. Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he said: "The auspiciousness of this original light makes even the Buddha Dīpaṃkara laugh to tears."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The osmanthus flowers scatter, autumn fills the mountain; We further invite the pure breeze for a sublime excursion.
Laughing at the hidden fragrance that turns beneath the leaves, The meaning of the Western Patriarch resides upon the branches. No evasion—how leisurely the inspiration!
The nostrils of the vast heavens are all pierced through; What place could one find that is not elegant?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The sword that kills, the blade that gives life—splitting empty space into two pieces. A thousand demons and a hundred monsters all hide their tracks;
the myriad phenomena of the universe manifest as light and shadow. As for the *ài-rén* (mugwort man) and the gate gods, do you truly see them or not?"
Holding up his staff, he said, "This staff provides a mere thread of passage.

On the occasion of the end of the summer retreat (*pravāraṇā*), he ascended the hall and said: "To have a binding and a releasing is to err in both; in the end, one is merely self-binding without a rope.

The ninety days of this summer retreat have concluded; for every one of you, eyebrows and whiskers have fallen away. Those who enter the water grow taller; those who fill the ditches and block the ravines—when we meet, there is only..."
"Jiānàsīqí! An enlightened-eyed monk need not engage in speculative calculation.
He ascended the hall and said: "As soon as one opens the mouth, it becomes superfluous talk; if one does not open the mouth, it becomes redundant speech.

To trigger the mechanism [of awakening], one must have a crossbow weighing a thousand *jūn*. The style of the thatched-roof shop is unique: it turns the clouds over and then covers them with rain. If it were Táo Yuánmíng... [He paused,] and the assembly crowded in.
Meibian returned home.
He ascended the hall and said: "Within the shadows of pine and vines, amidst heaps of gathered green, white clouds serve as a canopy and flowing springs act as a lute.
A solitary figure alone marks the moon upon the crag; who knows which person here is a true connoisseur? The ears are prickly, the head is disheveled—lift [your heads]!"
The hawk with piercing eyes flies over Liaodong.
He ascended the hall and said: "Speech and activity have no connection; yet speechlessness and inactivity likewise have no connection.
To empty my entrails and turn over my belly is to use one wedge to extract another. My mouth is silenced and my tongue is made bald; clearly, ten thousand miles away there is but a single path."
Iron. Entering the hall, he raised the verse by Hanshan: "When the autumn light is clear and shallow, the white heron blends with the misty isle;
how excellent is Avalokiteśvara, his whole body entering the wild grasses! Examining this closely, the transgressions are no small matter. Relying solely upon the staff, all—
He leaned against [his staff] and, leaning upon his staff, descended from the seat.
Entering the hall, he said: "Overturning the four great oceans, kicking over Mount Sumeru—coarse of heart and bold of spirit, with little substance and much emptiness.
Seeing the morning star at night, he once missed the mark; his descendants have followed after him, receiving only a smear of delusion."
The Anniversary of Songyuan’s Death. Autumn deepens as leaves fall and jade dew hangs low; I contemplate once more the solemnity of honoring the dead and remembering the distant past.

Without cause, you extinguished the race of Hu in a single lifetime; Bringing trouble upon your descendants—to whom can you speak of it? Muzzle shut! Eyebrows fallen! Dragging plows and pulling harrows, trailing water and mud.
To stroke a tiger’s whiskers and pick at a scorpion’s tail— Seeking advantage from the hands of a white-thief. The House.
"Fatness gives birth to filial sons; who is the child of the five rebellious acts? Today, Xi-xian makes this offering to his late teacher Songyuan.
Now tell me: will he come to partake of it or not? He shook his hand and said, "Ong yi, ong yi!
The message of autumn dew and spring wind remains; I know not who can present this supreme principle."
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zunsang of Yangshan in Pingjiang Prefecture, compiled by Attendant Fahong. Upon entering the monastery, he pointed to the Dharma seat and said:
"A shout scatters the white clouds; it pierces through the azure void. Even for Mount Sumeru and King Lamp, there is no place [to hide]."
Probing and searching.
He ascended the hall and said: "Deeply hidden in an ancient temple, old and decrepit; familiar with the warmth and cold, I know it only myself.
Yet, not having expected it, the official summons press me so hard that I must once again drag the plow."
When Elder Juebao went up to the hall, he said: "The door is opened to await the man of knowledge (jñānin), yet the man of knowledge does not come to pass through.

Now that the man of knowledge has indeed come to pass through, how ultimately shall one communicate the message? He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and said: "Opening the mouth is not a matter of the tongue;
wait and see the wind and waves arise upon level ground."

The evening informal discourse (xiaocan) said: "To control the mechanisms of the Buddhas and patriarchs, to blind the eyes of humans and devas, to employ phrases of life and death, and to cut through the thicket of entanglements—once the point is reached, there is no coming back, even from a thousand or ten thousand miles away. Therefore, the path above is slippery; it is as precipitous as a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms."
The spark from flint and the flash of lightning are dull; the phrase that settles heaven and earth is mistaken. This has been so from the beginning: setting up a target only to invite an arrow.
As for the honored aspect, there is a separate set of regulations: the Buddhas never appeared in the world, nor did they bestow a single dharma upon others.

Bodhidharma did not come from the West, and the Second Patriarch did not receive the marrow. To see a Buddha or a Patriarch is like encountering an enemy born of one's own kin; to speak of form or mind is likewise.
It is like encountering a fierce tiger. If one is a scaled dragon with crimson tails, as soon as they hear such a mention, they kick it up and go;
struck by a great club, they do not turn their heads back—dare anyone even look upon them with a direct eye? But if one is a dull bird perched on reeds, [it is otherwise].

In this way, they come in threes and twos. Why is it that "a former profligate feels a special affection for travelers"? It is because he loves those who crave the cup and cherishes those who are intoxicated.

[The Master] addressed the administrators and heads, saying in his ascent to the hall: "The great function of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is spread out before our very eyes. Within the host is the guest; within the guest..."

The Central Master [said]: "Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. Holding up his staff, he said: "To trigger the mechanism, one must have a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt.
New Year’s Eve Small Sermon: When the year ends and the time is exhausted, there is neither 'can' nor 'cannot. Cook the ox of the open field; burn the firewood of split logs.
A single spoonful of oil added to the vegetables; a bowl full of porridge for one meal’s satisfaction.

Laughing and swaggering amidst the mist and clouds, with white clouds brushing against the wind, he sings the "Song of Shaoyang" aloud to himself. When weary, he falls asleep, collapsing in his clothes.
Plowing deep and sowing shallow, he attains freedom; on the coral branches, the sun shines bright. Again, he raised the case where a monk asked an ancient worthy: "When the year ends and the age..."

"What is it like when [all things] are exhausted? Deyun replied: "The old king of the eastern village burns paper money at night. He then recited this verse: "The old king of the eastern village burns paper money at night;
Striking the south, it causes the north to shake. Bare-boned and utterly destitute, yet he boasts of wealth and honor;
When the sun has risen three *zhang* high, he still sleeps like a fool."
The vaulting sky reaches to the great void. Entering the hall, he said: "The old cat in the vaulting mountains—its single point of perfect luminosity blazes through the great void.
An octagonal millstone turns in the empty air; the secluded woods and springs possess a meaning all their own, transcending all material forms."
The model of "cutting off names" is about to become a red-bearded barbarian; there is yet another red-bearded barbarian. Entering the hall, he said:
"A monk asked Jingqing, 'In the deep mountains and rocky caves, is there still Buddha-dharma? Jingqing said, 'There is.
The monk asked, 'What is the Buddha-dharma in the deep mountains and rocky caves? He said, 'The boulder is large.'"
"Small, small. Or suppose someone comes forward and asks about his venerable appearance: "What is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky caves?
To him, he simply says, "None. Why is this so? It is simply because it is too near. He then recites a verse: "One person says there is; one person says there is not.
The true command is fully upheld in the talisman behind the elbow. Last night, empty space opened its mouth and laughed. The stone..."
"A person has swallowed Lake Dongting. He ascended the hall and said:
"Beyond the four propositions, transcending the hundred negations. Once a word has been uttered, even four horses cannot overtake it. Let the golden crow rise in the east as it will;
let the jade hare sink in the west as it must. He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and said: "A crossbow of a thousand *jin*..."
He set a trap for a field mouse. When the resident monks arrived, he ascended the hall and said:
"The spring rain is like rich cream; the spring clouds are like cranes. A guest comes from beyond the heavens—this is precisely the foot of the Demon King.
Within the threshold lies sovereign authority; the qilin has but a single horn. He struck his whisk and said: "A turn of the body—a sudden squeeze!"
Examining the source of these manifestations, even the externalists and celestial Māras lose their courage.
He ascended the hall and said: "The spring mountains are green; the spring waters are lush. Spring rain falls in misty drizzle; spring flowers cluster in profusion.
Spring light fills the eyes, a sight beyond painting. The spring breeze sweeps ten thousand miles—how can it be constrained? Fat horses roll along; lean horses roll along. Day..."
Chasing after busyness, one passes through life in negligence. Who could lightly touch this slight bit of poisonous vapor?
Entering the hall, he said: "Today is the first day of the fourth month; all phenomena cannot escape their shadows and substance. Mazu ascends the hall; Baizhang rolls up the mat.
Bimao wields his pitchfork; Luzu faces the wall. Calling a donkey a horse; a shrimp leaping out of the water—it cannot get out. Qilin...
The qilin has a single sharp horn; the turtle has three eyes that are red. Entering the hall, he said:
"The clouds have gathered at the edge of the heavens; the bright sun faces the void. Sitting and standing are solemn and still—how can one transmit this?
He struck his whisk and said: "From this point on, one need not go back; once one returns, it is attained. Amidst the misty waves of the Five Lakes, who would dare to compete?"
At the Lengyan Assembly, he ascended the hall and said: "The eight returns are resolved; the true eye opens at the crown of the head. Once awakened, every door has its Sudhana.
If you wish to know where the ninety-day practice of the Way takes place, the fragrant breeze still blows from the south as of old."
Everyone gathered together to visit him. He ascended the hall and said: "I cite the question posed to Master Mazu: 'Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
The questioner was like a venomous dragon churning the sea; the answerer was like a fierce tiger leaning against a mountain.
Although swift as a flash of lightning or a shooting star, they could not avoid remaining entirely outside the gate. Now tell me, how would one inside the gate explain this? He shifted his position.

Flowers arrive along with butterflies; buying stones, one gains an abundance of clouds. He then recited a verse: "Not to be a companion to the myriad dharmas— Biting down on the teeth, he errs in his citation.
The West River is sucked dry, yet the iron boat floats; A fierce dragon is seized alive and boiled with its horns."
Riding backward atop the Buddha hall, he emerges through the three gates; with one hand he turns them into clouds, with the other he brings down rain.
Entering the hall, he said: "Hares and horses have horns; oxen and sheep have no horns. Where wisdom does not reach, you must by all means refrain from speaking.
Once you have spoken, what then? He struck his whisk and said: "Having grasped the nostrils, you lose them again."
Ascending the hall at Yishou Peak, he said: "Meeting face-to-face, no brow is raised; thunder and lightning are slow to strike.

As soon as the one who knows tilts his ear, any deliberation falls into a disadvantage. Authority is exercised beyond the boundary; the wheel of the pivot is turned in a flash. He struck the meditation seat once and said:
"The great trichiliocosm is squeezed into a single mote of dust."
As Aotang ascended to the hall for the formal lecture, he said: "Xianan has passed away while his flesh is still warm; the five rebellious acts are returned to the son of the five rebellious acts.
At the peak of Haiyong, the true command is exercised—what audacious thief dares seek an advantage?"
On the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he ascended the hall and said: "I cite the words of Master Changsha: 'The entire earth is a single eye; the entire earth is a whole body.
The ten directions of the world are within one's own radiance. [He struck the meditation seat once.
If anyone can see this, the pure breeze will forever fill their seat; a single thought encompasses a hundred thousand years."
The Record of the Sermons at Shuangta Shouning Wansui Chan Monastery in Pingjiang Prefecture, compiled by the attendant Weidao. Ascending the hall:

Within the school of the patch-robed monks, one holds the sun and moon in hand, exercising supernatural powers; one bears Mount Sumeru on one’s back, manifesting the full functioning of the entire mechanism.

The enemy is victorious; the stars and constellations are shifted. Food is snatched away and the plowmen are driven off—how is this so? [The Master] strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and says:
"Were it not for the power of merit achieved through the toil of horses in sweat, how could one see the Yellow River clear to its very bottom?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Jueydu cited this: 'The ten directions have no walls; the four sides likewise have no gates.

Ultimately, where does one encounter the guest? If you can utter a phrase that takes up the hand [of the teaching], I grant you the heavens above and the heavens below. Shouning, however, is not like this:
the diamond circle and the jujube thorn—when brought forth, they are used immediately, illuminating the past and soaring through the present for those who know the Way beyond the categories."
As soon as it is experienced, a pure breeze arises from all four directions and eight corners.
Entering the hall, he said: "To have words within wordlessness is called a 'dead phrase. To have wordlessness within words is called a 'living phrase.

This can truly be described as carving a wound in one's own flesh until the skin is pierced and the bone is exposed. If you do not look back when the staff is raised, you will immediately miss the mark; it is like a flash of lightning."
The sun and moon race within;
he ascends the hall and says: "Before the fifteenth day, the wind cannot enter; after the fifteenth day, the water cannot wet."
"What is it like on the fifteenth day? [The Master] struck the meditation seat and said: "The immortal cassia tree in the moon is uprooted from its very base;
the mud ox at the bottom of the sea is led by the horns."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The nineteenth and twentieth days—people cannot believe it. He held up his whisk and said: 'To call this a whisk is to turn one's back on it;

not to call it a whisk is to commit an offense. Now, turning one's back and committing an offense are clearly evident. One phrase, perfectly clear, encompasses ten billion worlds. Tell me, what is that one phrase? Investigate!"* *Note: This is a traditional Zen kōan-style discourse. The "nineteenth and twentieth" likely refers to specific dates or stages of realization where conventional understanding fails.
"Turning one's back" (p'i) and "committing an offense" (ch'u) are technical terms for falling into dualistic extremes.*

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The heavens are cold and the people are cold; everyone is here. Washing one's face, one touches the nose; drinking tea, one wets the mouth. Is there anything further beyond this?
Or is there not? He struck the whisk and said: "This is the manner of Han Xin when he presided over the court."
The leader ascends the hall: On Mount Lu, at Huazang, by the shores of Lake Tai; with the pestle’s tip he pulls the sinew from within the eye.
Coming to take advantage of the heat of the hearth at Shouning, he strides alone through the great thousand-fold world, beholding the soaring path of the Peng bird.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Wisdom is not the Way; the mind is not the Buddha. Rolling the Xuefeng ball, dancing with the Daowu staff—tell me, what matter on this side of reality does this clarify?
Shaking his hand, he said: "Not saying, not saying."
The former acquaintance Daojiu arrived. He ascended the hall and said: "The second month, spring has passed its half; gardens and groves are all renewed.

Beside the flowers, one watches the butterflies dance; near the willows, one listens to the orioles sing. A traveler from afar comes to visit—has he ever awakened to this mind? Lin Zhengzhen plants crabapples at the bottom of the well.
This year, peaches and plums are precious; a single fruit is worth a thousand pieces of gold."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva went to buy a fried cake with his money; when he let it go, it turned out to be a steamed bun.
Beating time at the banquet, looking down from the tower to strike the tower. (He strikes the whisk) Even where there is no elegance, there is elegance."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The warbling of swallows and the singing of orioles both discourse upon the true mark (*dharmatā*). The spring breeze stirs the peach and plum blossoms;

thin mist and sparse rain enshroud the green peaks. Having finished speaking, he asked, "Do you understand? Striking the meditation seat, he said: "Above all, do not try to imitate the model or paint the likeness."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In Guizong, both phenomena and principle are cut off; the sun is at its zenith at noon. The sackcloth bag wears a look of foolishness; the cat catches the mouse.
If anyone can understand this, they transcend Buddhas and surpass patriarchs. He struck his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Great Way extends horizontally and vertically; it is manifest before our very eyes. Sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
Look, look! But tell me, ultimately does it turn left or turn right? Last night someone came from Huzhou bringing news from Huainan. The Great Sage of Sizhou says:
'The stone statue in Wuzhong ought not to swallow Lake Dongting whole.'"
The lake. It would have to be such that Mount Sumeru is overturned and planted upright, and the waters of the ocean flow backward. But tell me, what matter of realization does this clarify?
*Chan*. A Verse on the Ancient Case: Zhaozhou Meets Two Hermitages.
The southern branches face the warmth, while the northern branches are cold; a single spring breeze manifests in two different ways. I send word to those atop high towers:
do not blow your flutes; let us all preserve the space to lean against the balustrade.

When the non-Buddhists questioned the Buddha while harboring a precious mirror within their chests, the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time as if holding it aloft; they were like fine horses catching a glimpse of the whip’s shadow,
unaware that their entire bodies had already fallen into the Iron Ring Mountains.
The opening of the mouth is not upon the tongue;
openly repairing the plank road while secretly crossing Chen’ang Pass. Marking the boat while still searching for the sword; the night rain passes over Xiao and Xiang.
A man of great power cannot lift his feet.
Only the old barbarian is permitted to know; the old barbarian is not permitted to understand. Where the white clouds end, there are green mountains;
the traveler is further beyond the green mountains.
For one of great power, the red thread beneath their feet is never severed.
Releasing two and tossing three; deceiving gods and shouting at ghosts. Exchanging one basin for another—whom does he not know?
Mount Huai’s movement of the sun follows its course;
Mount Huai’s raising of a son has no underlying reason. Folding his hands before others, he knows no shame; he even uses a lute to half-conceal himself.
His face does not allow others to see it turn;
Nanquan’s “beheading of the cat” is like a sharp sword cutting down a marten—did he turn over in his tracks beneath the blade? Take off your straw sandals and place them upon your head.
Emerging, a stone man swallows Lake Dongting.
A Dharma talk sent to the layman Yan Yiqi.

Last month, I was specially honored by your dispatching a messenger with gifts of incense and tokens of faith. You presented me with your teachings, which have been of great benefit for over ten years.
I have focused my attention here, and only now have I reached the point of entry; the phrasing is extraordinary. It is already evident that you possess swift and skillful mastery.
When one first perceives it in this way, having now attained the point of entry, it is like a person drinking a crude liquor made from straw;
after a short while, it suddenly disperses and vanishes again. Nevertheless, one has nonetheless found the place where one can set foot and hand.
One should simply proceed from the ground already attained, making it firm and stable like a single wall of iron or a mountain of silver.
Master, from this point on there will be great illumination, and only then will you experience the fulfillment of your life. Furthermore, there is another saying:

if one realizes what is before one's eyes but does not realize one's own self, it is called "having feet but no eyes. If one realizes one's own self but does not realize what is before one's eyes, it is called "having eyes but no feet.
When one thoroughly penetrates both of these extremes, then the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings are all—

Upon a single hair-tip, there are a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes. Only when one reaches this point does the Great Dharma become luminous in all places, penetrating the ancient and modern koans of apparent contradiction.
Yet, one must still encounter a person to truly attain it. Therefore, the mind of *nirvāṇa* is easy to understand, but the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify.
If you wish to penetrate and transcend birth and death, you need only rely on the final segment of the teaching under the Gate.
When you are about to leave the precipice, it is precisely at this place devoid of flavor that you must apply effort. Beneath great doubt, there will surely be great awakening.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, maintain a resolute will; you will certainly not be deceived.
Of the seventy virtuous teachers (kalyāṇamitra) whom the ancients encountered, only one or two possessed the great eye of insight; the rest merely possessed correct knowledge and vision.
Within the vehicle of our school, it is difficult to find those with great means who can pull out the nails and extract the wedges for others.

If you can resolve to devote this entire life to practice without seeking results, then where there is intention, there is no attainment; yet, by being free of such intent, you will ultimately be brought to completion under the guidance of the lineage.
Through a thousand lives and ten thousand rebirths, may you attain great freedom. May all practitioners most earnestly whip themselves on—this would be a blessing.
Although you have managed to enter the "place of the head," rejoice for now; your spirit and breath are stabilized and motionless, so external demons cannot easily intrude.

However, you must investigate and pursue whatever doubts remain in your breast. At midnight, enter the divine essence and examine it thoroughly. It is empty yet spiritual, still yet wondrous. There is great rest and profound repose—no wonder more wondrous than this, no depth more profound than this.
Be prepared to devote your entire life to this with resolute intent, and realize this single point of spiritual clarity.

Experience will surely not prove you wrong; yet I fear that when you reach a point where there is no further recourse, you might fail to press forward, thereby rendering all your prior efforts in vain.
You must by no means allow your resolve to falter. It is precisely in those moments when things seem devoid of flavor that you should exert yourself; only then do you become a person of great power.

Regarding all words and phrases, setting aside external objects is superior, while chasing after objects is inferior. Above all, take care not to let the mind give rise to conceptualizations based on words.
[The Master] said: "This is a great illness.

The clashing and knocking within the chamber is sufficient to fill it. Since this matter is as earnest as this, there is no one throughout all quarters who does not discern and awaken to the gateway of the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, I hope you will reach the state where not a single thought arises, wherein the whole body functions; therein lies the subtle and minute."

Only after grinding it to a fine point through exhaustive inquiry will you know that essence and function are both complete, and that going and staying are at ease. Do not merely listen to the clever words of others;
you must possess your own power of concentration to achieve this.
Studying Chan is for the great matter of penetrating and transcending birth and death; it is not for practicing "verbal Chan" in order to seek food and clothing.
One must directly set aside body and mind, step back to examine oneself, and never miss a single point. As the saying goes: "Coarse food is easily satiated."
Even if one chews food slowly, hunger remains; this is not yet knowing. When one knows, it is as if one has lost one’s parents.
If what is within the breast is not clear, one must not recklessly act as an elder or claim to be a *kalyāṇamitra*. This is what is meant by "the numinous tortoise bearing the map."
You are bringing upon yourself the omen of losing your very life; you must take care with utmost urgency. Once this human body is lost, it will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas.
Rather than spending a lifetime in vain, burying your head among the masses, you must rescue yourself.

This great treasury of radiant light is attained in this present life, and for hundreds and thousands of future lives, you shall naturally enjoy its benefits. The mind is the sovereign; if the master is deluded, the guest takes over.

Taking advantage of the moment, he would occasionally draw his precious sword, the Vajra King. As soon as it was raised upward or downward, he would briefly strike and cut [the opponent] into three pieces;
he was truly impetuous by nature. If this were not so, do not let your idle scholarly interpretations bury the mind of the Patriarch.
Entrusting this face to the silent chamber within the One-Zhai Hall, Master Fang’s "Mind is Buddha" is free from confusion.
Without moving the tongue, his spirit abounds; he breaks through empty space to travel the living path, and husband and wife clap their hands in joyful laughter.
Entrusting the bamboo whisk to Chief Seat Jingche:

"Bamboo whisk! Bamboo whisk! Having bestowed it, what is there further to do? The Buddhas and Patriarchs brandish it directly before one's face. With a mere span of water, one can overturn the surging waves;
let people exhaust themselves in seeking the mechanism that cuts across the current.
Shen Anqi styled himself "Ever-Pasturing" at his thatched hut;
yet he still fell into the trap of merit and was not free. This is no different from lying in stagnant water like a mud-dwelling ox.
How much better it would be to take a wide stride forward from the tip of the fishing pole—to cast off one's hands atop a precipice ten thousand fathoms high!

Self-praise beneath Mount Zixiao: using poison to counteract poison, scattering earth and hurling sand, twisting the straight into the crooked, shaking the four great continents and overturning the earth’s axis with a single punch and kick.
This Chan of inherent nature has met with its time of decline; one must strictly avoid vainly shouting instructions into the empty air.
Seated atop the peaks of a thousand mountains, he turns his head to listen to empty sounds at will.
With a blade as sharp as a hair, he brandishes it horizontally and fully maintains the orthodox command. Destroying Buddhas and slandering the Dharma, he strikes the upright because of the perverse;
sometimes he tears off his own face-skin, leaving the monks of the world begging for their lives.
Within seventy-eight years since his departure from this world, inner and outer emptiness—casting off all attachments, he has walked forth; a pure breeze for all eternity.
On the day of Yichou in the eighth month of the Xinchou year of Chunyou, the monk Taibai Mingshan, Tiao Chong, respectfully proofread [this].
The Recorded Sayings of Master Wuming (Concluded).
Epitaph composed and calligraphed by Yan Ruxun, *Digonglang* and *Zhubu* of Yongjia County, Wenzhou.
Chao Sanlang Fang Wanli, serving as the Military and Civil Governor of Xinzhou, inscribed these characters for the plaque.
This Way possesses a direct lineage; it is simply that there is not even a trace of worldly breath within it. It is indeed close to the ultimate, and one who knows it can approach this closeness.
This means that if one holds that the true pulse resides within this, it is delusion. To meet it, it does not linger; to let it go, it is not abandoned.

As rain falls in the north and clouds gather in the south, as the Dipper shifts and the stars change, if one forgets to maintain it or loses its illumination, how could the wondrous even stand? When a spring rushes to the mountain peak, seeking its source is but dead water;
when hail falls from the blue sky, following its trace is but adventitious dust. If you intend to knit your brows, your chin will jut forward; if you wish to laugh, your expression will contract.
The pivot of the sliding bolt turned, and heaven and earth grew dark. Although the dragon-gods had long sworn to protect him, they ultimately found no place to do so.
This Master shook his hands back and forth with a creaking sound for a long time, unable to stop himself. I knew then that he was the ninth-generation descendant of Yangqi.
